title: Act IV, Scene I

teacherSummary.text: Gertrude tells Claudius that Hamlet, mad, killed Polonius. Claudius realizes it could have been him and resolves to ship Hamlet away at once, and to manage public opinion.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act IV, Scene I,” how does Shakespeare show Claudius hears of Polonius's death? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act IV, Scene I, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of Claudius hears of Polonius's death? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act IV, Scene I develops the idea of Claudius hears of Polonius's death. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and plot shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act IV, Scene I (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of Claudius hears of Polonius's death. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act IV, Scene I suggests about Claudius hears of Polonius's death. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's characterization and plot), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses characterization in Act IV, Scene I to complicate the reader's understanding of Claudius hears of Polonius's death. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act IV, Scene I within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of Claudius hears of Polonius's death responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act IV, Scene I alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of Claudius hears of Polonius's death follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act IV, Scene I and its treatment of Claudius hears of Polonius's death. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's characterization and plot, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act IV, Scene I as evidence for a larger claim about Claudius hears of Polonius's death in Hamlet. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act IV, Scene I as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of Claudius hears of Polonius's death. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Hamlet.

symbolsAndMotifs.name: disease and rot
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: Denmark is sick: "Something is rotten in the state of Denmark"; corruption spreads like poison and ulcers. In this scene: “was most fit; / But, like the owner of a foul disease, / To keep it from divulging, let it feed / Even on the” (Act IV, Scene I, King (speech 5)).
symbolsAndMotifs.quote: was most fit; / But, like the owner of a foul disease, / To keep it from divulging, let it feed / Even on the

symbolsAndMotifs.name: poison and ears
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: Old Hamlet was poisoned through the ear; lies poured into ears, and poison returns at the end. In this scene: “As level as the canon to his blank, / Transports his poison’d shot, may miss our name, / And hit the woundless air. O” (Act IV, Scene I, speech (speech 7)).

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.

Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: Claudius's response shows concern for his own safety. Useful evidence: “Come, Gertrude, we’ll call up our wisest friends” (Act IV, Scene I, speech (speech 7)): Claudius's political move. Theme link: Claudius worries about public opinion. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
